content: CD1, also known as cluster of differentiation 1, refers to a family of glycoproteins that are expressed on the surface of various human antigen-presenting cells. These glycoproteins are structurally related to class I major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules and are involved in presenting lipid antigens to T cells. However, the precise biological function of CD1 molecules remains unclear. CD1 glycoproteins are categorized into two primary groups based on their lipid anchoring properties. Group 1 CD1 molecules, which include CD1a, CD1b, and CD1c, are expressed on cells that are specialized for antigen presentation. In contrast, Group 2 CD1 molecules, represented by CD1d, are expressed on a broader range of cell types. CD1e is an intermediate form that is expressed intracellularly, but its role is not yet well understood. In humans, Group 1 CD1 molecules have been shown to present foreign lipid antigens, including specific components of the mycobacterial cell wall, to CD1-specific T cells. On the other hand, the natural antigens for Group 2 CD1 molecules are not well characterized. However, a synthetic glycolipid known as alpha-galactosylceramide, originally isolated from a compound found in marine sponges, exhibits strong biological activity. Group 2 CD1 molecules activate a subset of T cells called natural killer T (NKT) cells, which are characterized by the expression of NK surface markers such as CD161. NKT cells are activated by antigens presented by CD1d and rapidly produce both Th1 and Th2 cytokines, including interferon-gamma and interleukin-4 (IL-4). Notably, the Group 2 (CD1d) ligand alpha-galactosylceramide is currently undergoing phase I clinical trials for the treatment of advanced non-hematologic cancers. From a diagnostic perspective, CD1 antigens are expressed on cortical thymocytes but are absent on mature T cells. This pattern often persists in neoplastic cells derived from these populations, making the presence of CD1 antigens a useful marker in diagnostic immunohistochemistry. For example, CD1 antigens can help identify certain thymomas and malignancies arising from T cell precursors. Specifically, CD1a serves as a distinct marker for Langerhans cells and is therefore valuable in diagnosing Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Other conditions that may exhibit CD1 positivity include myeloid leukemia and certain B cell lymphomas. In mice, Group 1 CD1 molecules are absent, and instead, mice possess two copies of CD1d. This makes mice a widely used model for studying the role of CD1d and CD1d-dependent NKT cells in various disease contexts. Conversely, cows lack Group 2 CD1 molecules but have an expanded repertoire of Group 1 CD1 molecules. Given that cows are a natural host for Mycobacterium bovis, a pathogen that also infects humans, studying the CD1 antigen-presenting system in cows may provide valuable insights into the function of Group 1 CD1 molecules.
